title: Prompting power
content_html:
What You'll Do

Getting a great answer out of an AI chatbot like ChatGPT is a skill, not luck. Most people type a short, vague request, get a boring answer, and decide "the AI isn't very good." In this project you'll prove the opposite: you'll run the same request three times, making it more specific each time, and watch the answers go from generic to genuinely useful.

By the end you'll have made your own Prompt Recipe Card — a simple formula you can reuse any time — and used it to solve a real request of your own, like a birthday party idea, a study plan, or a story. The big idea: the quality of your question shapes the quality of the AI's answer.

What You'll Need

  • ChatGPT (free) — https://chat.openai.com. You'll need to sign in with an email or Google account. At busy times it may say it's "busy" — just refresh or wait about 30 seconds.
  • No ChatGPT? You can do the whole project on Microsoft Copilot — https://copilot.microsoft.com — or Google Gemini — https://gemini.google.com.
  • Somewhere to write — paper or a doc — to make your Prompt Recipe Card (four columns: Role / Task / Detail / Format) and to save your best prompts.
  • Good to know: on the free tools you might hit message limits when lots of people are online, and answers can be slow if many devices share the same Wi-Fi. If it's slow, be patient or team up with a friend on one device.

Steps

  1. Before you start, make a guess: what do you think you'll get if you ask ChatGPT Tell me about dogs compared with a very specific question? Jot down your guess.
  2. Open ChatGPT (or Copilot / Gemini) and type this exact vague prompt: Tell me about dogs. Read the answer.
  3. Ask yourself: is this actually useful? What's missing? Who is this answer written for? (Probably no one in particular — that's the problem.)
  4. Learn the 4-part Prompt Recipe: Role (who should the AI pretend to be?), Task (what exactly do you want?), Detail (context, who it's for, any limits), Format (a list, a story, a table, a short paragraph).
  5. Try the recipe on the dog question. Type: You are a vet. Explain to a curious 10-year-old why dogs wag their tails, in 3 fun facts with emojis. Compare this answer with your first one — spot the difference?
  6. Now pick your own topic — a hobby, a school subject, a problem you have — and write a Level 1 prompt (vague, one sentence). Run it.
  7. Write a Level 2 prompt on the same topic using the full 4-part recipe. Run it.
  8. Write a Level 3 prompt by adding one more rule — a word limit, a tone, or an example format — to push the answer even further. Run it.
  9. Fill in your Prompt Recipe Card with your best Level 3 prompt, and save your favourite answer next to it.
  10. Look back at your Level 1 and your Level 3 prompt side by side. In one sentence, write down what changed and why the answer got better.

Examples to Try

  • Level 1: "Help me plan a party." → a generic list with no context.
    Level 3: "You are an event planner. Plan a budget-friendly 12th birthday party for 15 kids in Nairobi, with an outdoor theme, under KES 5,000. Give me a table with activity, time, and cost." → a real table with local activities, timings and costs.
  • Level 1: "Tell me about the water cycle." → a dense, textbook-style paragraph.
    Level 3: "You are a fun science teacher. Explain the water cycle to a 9-year-old using a short story about a raindrop named Dudu, in 5 sentences." → a fun mini-story that's easy to remember.
  • Level 1: "Give me a study plan." → a vague, one-size-fits-all list.
    Level 3: "You are a study coach. Create a 5-day revision timetable for a Grade 7 student preparing for a Maths exam on fractions and decimals, with 30-minute sessions and one fun break each day. Present it as a table." → a clear, personal schedule you could actually follow.

Tips

  • Specific beats long. A short, precise prompt almost always beats a long, rambling one. Don't just add more words — add the right details.
  • Got a weird or wrong answer? That's normal — AI doesn't always get it right the first time. Instead of giving up, ask yourself "what could I add or change?" and try again.
  • Make it yours. Don't copy someone else's prompt — pick a topic you actually care about, so the answer is useful to you.
  • Keep it private. Anything you type into the chat isn't secret. Never put your real full name, home address, or school details into a prompt.
  • If writing from a blank page feels hard, start your Recipe Card as fill-in-the-blanks: "You are a ___. Help me ___. It's for ___. Give it to me as a ___."

Think About It

  • What's the difference between a "vague" prompt and a "specific" one? Give an example of each.
  • Why do you think giving the AI a "role" (like "you are a vet") changes its answer?
  • Was there a moment when even a detailed prompt gave you a wrong answer? What did you do next?
  • Can a prompt be "too detailed" or "too long"? What do you think?
  • How is asking a good question to an AI like — or different from — asking a good question to a teacher or a friend?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Take one Level 3 prompt and change only the format (ask for a poem instead of a list). See how differently the same information comes out.
  • Medium: Write a prompt that asks for two styles at once — "Explain this first like I'm 5, then like I'm 15" — and compare them.
  • Hard: Build a prompt chain: three prompts in a row where each builds on the AI's last answer (ask for a story idea, then turn it into a script, then ask for a title and a moral). Show your final result and explain how each prompt shaped the next.
